title: Postgres VACUUM FULL on a 500GB table — how do I avoid a six-hour exclusive lock?
body: We have a heavily-bloated 500GB table and VACUUM FULL is holding the exclusive lock for way too long during our maintenance window. Is there a safer online approach that doesn't take the database offline for hours? I've looked at pg_repack but haven't used it in production yet.

answers.body: pg_repack is the standard answer. It rebuilds the table under a trigger-based shadow copy so writes keep flowing. Schedule it during low traffic and watch your WAL usage.
Alternative: partition the table by created_at, then drop and rebuild old partitions. Doesn't help for hot data but works great for archival.

title: How do I profile a Go service with pprof in production without pausing it?
body: We run a Go service under continuous load and I need CPU profiles from production to chase a latency regression. Restarting to enable pprof isn't an option — the service is critical. Is `net/http/pprof` safe to leave running behind auth, or should I use something like `runtime/pprof` with a signal handler instead? Looking for the least-invasive approach that doesn't add measurable overhead when idle.

answers.body: `net/http/pprof` is fine in production as long as you bind it to a separate internal port and gate it with your usual auth. The endpoints only consume CPU while a profile is being taken — when idle they cost nothing measurable.

Also consider `runtime/trace` for the latency question specifically. pprof tells you where CPU time goes; trace tells you where wall-clock time goes, which is often the real answer for a latency regression.

title: What's the right way to version a REST API that has mobile clients you can't force-update?
body: We have an iOS and Android app in the wild that we can't force-update — users on old versions will keep hitting our API for months. I'm weighing URL versioning (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) against header versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2`). The header approach feels cleaner in theory but I keep imagining support tickets where someone forgets to send the right header. What has actually worked for you in production with slow-moving mobile clients?
